findings.evidence: core.py:99 `f"/repos/{REPO}/commits/{head}/statuses"` vs stuck_alerts.py:189 `f"/repos/{REPO}/commits/{head}/statuses?per_page=100"`; both select a context and take `sort_by(.updated_at) | last`.
findings.fix: Put one generic `newest_status(head, context)` (with per_page=100) in core; have core.ci_status call it and normalize pending/success/failure→its states, and have stuck_alerts import newest_status from core instead of defining its own.
findings.issue: core.ci_status reads `/repos/{REPO}/commits/{head}/statuses`, selecting context=="build" and taking the newest by updated_at — the same 'newest commit status for a context' logic stuck_alerts.newest_status (stuck_alerts.py:182) already implements in the same package (now that stuck_alerts imports core). This is exactly the kind of residual duplication this refactor is meant to remove, and the two have already diverged: newest_status uses `?per_page=100` (documented as necessary so a burst of status events can't push `build` off the default first page) while ci_status omits it.

summary: The core extraction is a genuine net de-duplication and the two sinks correctly share core.derive with no leftover copies. One residual near-clone remains: core.ci_status re-implements the newest-status-for-a-context read that stuck_alerts.newest_status already provides in the same package, and the two have already diverged.
